segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Looking intently at the council, Paul said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Brothers, I have conducted my life before God in all good conscience up to this day.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the high priest Ananias ordered those standing beside him to strike him on the mouth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Paul said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall! You sit there judging me according to the Law, and yet in violation of the Law you order me to be struck?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those standing by said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Are you insulting God’s high priest?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I did not know, brothers, that he is the high priest; for it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Realizing that one faction was made up of Sadducees and the other of Pharisees, Paul cried out in the council,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. It is concerning the hope and the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was saying this, a conflict broke out between the Pharisees and Sadducees, and the assembly was split.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Sadducees say there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit, but Pharisees affirm them all.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A great outcry arose, and some of the scribes of the Pharisees’ faction stood up and argued fiercely, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We find nothing wrong in this man. What if a spirit has spoken to him, or an angel—”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As the conflict grew fierce, the tribune, fearing that Paul would be torn apart by them, ordered the troops to go down, snatch him from among them, and bring him into the barracks.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The following night the Lord stood by him and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Take courage! For just as you have testified fully about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify in Rome as well.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When day came, the Jews banded together and bound themselves under a curse, saying that they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There were more than forty who formed this conspiracy.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They went to the chief priests and the elders and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We have bound ourselves under a solemn curse to taste nothing until we have killed Paul.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So now you, together with the council, notify the tribune to bring him down to you, as though you were going to examine his case more closely. As for us, we are ready to kill him before he gets near.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the son of Paul’s sister heard about the ambush, and he came and entered the barracks and reported it to Paul.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul called one of the centurions and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to report to him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he took him and brought him to the tribune and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The prisoner Paul called me over and asked me to bring this young man to you, since he has something to say to you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The tribune took him by the hand, drew him aside privately, and asked,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What is it that you have to report to me?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though it were going to inquire somewhat more closely about him.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So do not be persuaded by them, for more than forty of their men are lying in ambush for him. They have bound themselves under a curse neither to eat nor to drink until they have killed him, and now they are ready, waiting for your promise.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the tribune dismissed the young man, ordering him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Tell no one that you have notified me of this.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he called two of the centurions and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Get two hundred soldiers ready to go as far as Caesarea, along with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen, starting at the third hour of the night.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Provide mounts as well, so that they can put Paul on them and bring him safely through to Felix the governor.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He wrote a letter to this effect:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Claudius Lysias, to the most excellent governor Felix: greetings.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the troops and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman citizen.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Wanting to know the charge on which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I found that he was being accused over disputed points of their law, but faced no charge deserving death or chains.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: When it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once, and I also ordered his accusers to state their case against him before you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the soldiers, in keeping with their orders, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The next day they let the horsemen go on with him and returned to the barracks.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the horsemen entered Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they also presented Paul to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After reading it, he asked what province he was from, and on learning that he was from Cilicia, he said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I will hear your case when your accusers have arrived as well.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he ordered that he be kept under guard in Herod’s praetorium.

notes.note: The verb originally described living as a citizen and discharging public duties, and some translations bring that out (“fulfilled my duty to God”). By this period it was also used more generally for how a person conducts his life, especially in Jewish Greek writing about living by God’s law. The rendering keeps the more general sense; a civic overtone is possible but cannot be shown.

The image is of a shaky wall given a coat of whitewash to hide its condition, and many scholars hear an echo of Ezekiel 13:10–15, where God promises to bring such a wall down. Ananias son of Nedebaeus was high priest from about AD 47 to 59. Ordering an accused man struck before any finding of guilt went against the Law’s demand for fair judgment.

It is disputed whether Paul means this literally (the hearing was irregular, convened by a Roman officer, and he may not have recognized who gave the order) or ironically, implying that a man who behaves this way is not acting as a high priest. The Greek allows either. The quotation is from Exodus 22:28.

notes.phrase: the hope and the resurrection of the dead
notes.traditional: the hope and resurrection of the dead
notes.note: The Greek joins two nouns with “and.” Many interpreters take this as a single idea, “the hope of the resurrection of the dead,” and several translations render it that way. The text keeps the two nouns as the Greek has them; the sense is much the same either way.

The Greek word normally means “both,” but in the Greek of this period it could be used of more than two (as in Acts 19:16). If it means “both” here, the two things are resurrection on one side and angel-or-spirit on the other. Some scholars instead read “angel” and “spirit” as describing forms of the resurrected state that the Sadducees denied.

notes.traditional: let us not fight against God
notes.note: In the earliest manuscripts the sentence breaks off unfinished, as if drowned out by the uproar. Later manuscripts complete it with “let us not fight against God,” probably borrowed from Acts 5:39; the King James Version follows that longer text.

The Greek title, literally “commander of a thousand,” was the standard equivalent of the Roman military tribune. This officer commanded the cohort stationed in the Antonia fortress overlooking the temple, which is the “barracks” of this chapter. Some translations use the more general “commander.”

Many modern translations say the men took an “oath,” but the verb is stronger: they called down a curse on themselves, declaring themselves devoted to destruction, if they failed to carry out the vow. The older English tradition (“bound themselves under a curse”) is closer to the Greek. In verse 14 the Greek doubles the word for emphasis, rendered there as “a solemn curse.”

The meaning of this word is uncertain. It is found nowhere else in surviving Greek of this period and only rarely centuries later. It seems to name some kind of light-armed soldier; “spearmen” is the conventional guess, and others have suggested slingers, bowmen or local auxiliaries.

notes.phrase: the third hour of the night
notes.traditional: the third hour of the night
notes.note: Night hours were counted from sunset, so this is about nine in the evening. The size of the escort, nearly half the garrison, shows how seriously the tribune took the threat.

notes.phrase: having learned that he was a Roman citizen
notes.traditional: having learned that he was a Roman
notes.note: The letter presents events in the order most flattering to its writer. According to Acts 21:31–39 and 22:24–29, Lysias learned of Paul’s citizenship only after he had arrested him, put him in chains and ordered him flogged, none of which the letter mentions.
Many later manuscripts close the letter with the customary “Farewell.” The earliest witnesses lack it, and the SBLGNT omits it.

A praetorium was the official residence and headquarters of a Roman governor. In Caesarea the governors used the palace built by Herod the Great, so Paul was held in the governor’s own compound, not in a common prison. Felix’s question about Paul’s province in verse 34 was to establish whether he had jurisdiction over the case.

candidates.reason: Translations vary between “council” and “Sanhedrin” across the Gospels and Acts, and readers would be confused if the same body were named differently from chapter to chapter.
Rendered variously as “tribune,” “commander” and “chief captain”; it recurs through Acts 21–25 and in John, Mark and Revelation, and should be uniform.
Occurs in the passion narratives, Acts and Philippians 1:13 with renderings ranging from “palace” and “headquarters” to “praetorium” and “imperial guard”; one policy is needed.
The verb and its noun ἀνάθεμα recur in Mark 14:71, Romans 9:3, 1 Corinthians and Galatians 1:8–9, where “oath,” “curse” and “accursed” compete.
Very frequent in the Gospels and Acts; “scribes,” “teachers of the law” and “experts in the Law” are all in use, and the choice should be made once.
